I see a lot of complaints that the Electoral College is "undemocratic" and is only enabling a "tyranny of the minority" instead of a "tyranny of the majority". These arguments miss the point of the Electoral College, which is to make sure that nobody gets to be a tyrant. Allow me to explain:

Consider states like New York and California. These states have such a large population that just a handful of them constitutes a popular majority. If the president were elected by popular vote, candidates would spend an inordinate amount of time wooing them. However, under the electoral college system, you get the same number of EC votes from these states when you have 51% of their populations' vote as you would if you had 100%. This gives candidates an incentive to try to make people from other states happy. If you know you're "safe" in New York because you can expect 60% of the vote there, then you gain nothing by expending your campaign resources trying to woo the other 40%. It only makes sense to go campaign somewhere else. Not so under a popular voting system.

This isn't only important during elections--if not for the Electoral College, political parties would be trying to woo the voters of places like Texas, New York, Florida, and California year round. Smaller states could kiss their federal funding goodbye. They'll be taxed just as heavily, sure, but they shouldn't expect to ever see most of that money again. Their votes just aren't worth the trouble. Why come up with a diverse platform of ideas that serves as many people as possible when you can just get 100% of the city slickers on your side?

Side note: This effect is diminished in states that allow a split electoral vote, which is why "winner take all" is actually a good thing. Winner take all is designed to tell the candidates "You win, now GTFO and go hear somebody else's issues".

tl;dr: The EC makes sure everybody gets something from a candidate, instead of a majority getting everything and the rest getting nothing.
